Dorado Academy 
High School Science Department 
Plant The Moon Challenge 2023-2024 
Advisor: Mrs. Verónica Ortiz Berríos 
Team Name: Space Monkeys 
Team ID Number: 17126 
 
Team Information: Dorado Academy. Dorado, Puerto Rico 
Students: Ramón Arroyo, Antonio Valentín, Antonio Tavárez, Daniel Irrizary, Edwin Almodovar, Emil 
Rodríguez, Fabián Gómez, Fabián Santiago, Ginarelle Bermúdez 
Teacher: Mrs. Verónica Ortiz Berríos 
 
PTMC: Optimizing Water Retention by using Kokedama method. 
 
Background information 
Numerous studies confirm the positive influence of green spaces on people's well-being, not only as urban 
lungs, but particularly in hospitals, workplaces, and educational centers and, of course, in space stations. 
From all the ideas we considered for this experiment we chose how to optimize plant water retention by 
changing the traditional planting method and replacing it with a kokedama. We believe this would have a 
great impact as it could reduce the amount of water needed to growth a plant in space. 
The Kokedama originate from Japan; they are derived from the bonsai. Plants are grown in moss-covered, 
spherical balls made of soil and secured under the handmade "fabric" of rope. This natural covering, moss, 
and rope, acts as a pot and allows oxygenation of the roots. 
The moss in a kokedama is not only its container, nor its decoration. The moss is capable of retaining 
several times its weight in water; moisture is released little by little, nourishing the inside of the ball as the 
roots of the plant demand water. In addition, the moss prevents the substrate from being washed away 
during watering. 
However, in our experiment we also used coconut fibers. Coir, also known as coconut fiber, is becoming 
popular as an environmentally responsible and sustainable plant growth medium. This natural material, 
which comes from the husk of coconuts, is used in gardening due to its versatile uses and beneficial 
purposes. Because coconut fiber holds water so well, it's a great material for plants that need constant 
moisture. The root system won't over dry out thanks to its moisture retention, which lessens the need for 
frequent watering. Furthermore, it fosters more robust root development by preserving a constant 
moisture content. Coconut fiber not only helps plants retain water, but it also gives their roots efficient air
tables: Rodríguez, Fabián Gómez, Fabián Santiago, Ginarelle Bermúdez

pages.text:
circulation. It maintains a balance between air circulation and moisture retention, which is essential for 
keeping roots supplied with oxygen and avoiding root rot. Since coconut fiber has no pH of its own, mixing 
it with soil or growing it in a medium won't cause it to change the pH of the mixture much. 
In the following experiment we will be utilizing a mixture of a nutrient deficient substance known as lunar 
regolith as a growing medium for our plants. Regolith, more commonly known as sediment, is the result 
of the weathering of bedrock. Since there is no wind or running water on the moon for weathering to take 
place, lunar regolith is formed by meteorite collisions and solar wind. The grains of regolith vary in size 
depending on their maturity. The maturity is dependent on the length of time it has been exposed to the 
solar wind and meteorite environment. If lunar regolith was to be compared to soil it would be the most 
like sand, due to its porous nature and fine particles. To alleviate the deficiency in water retention and 
nutrients we decided to mix the substance with garden soil. 
Garden soil is a combination of topsoil and organic matter. The reason garden soil was chosen over potting 
soil was mainly because of garden soil’s innate ability to improve soil texture. According to our research it 
may prove counterproductive to use potting soil because of its high drainage. Garden soil on the other 
hand, has been proven to have the capacity to retain a significant amount of water and nutrients. Since 
the goal of our experiment is the test for water retention, we wanted to maximize the amount of water 
that is being retained by the plants. 
The seed we grew was the Black seeded Simpson. This seed falls under the category of Garden Lettuce 
(Lactuca Sativa). It was chosen for qualities such as its bolting resistance. Although, it was primarily chosen 
because it germinates quickly and has been shown to grow in previous regolith experiments. The plant 
also does not need too much water, so it is easier to manage for people that have not grown plants before. 
Again, we are trying to optimize the water retention method, so we need to have a plant that we already 
know could grow in regolith. 
Hypothesis 
By using the kokedama planting method, we expect that the water retention will increase due to the 
moss and coconut fibers shell absorption properties, which will lead to the plant needing less water to 
grow.

Materials-Lamps, pots, garden soil, coconut fiber, moss fiber, regolith, fishing string, measuring 
cup, electronica balance, graduated cylinder, spray bottle, soil master, skewer, ruler, seeds. 
Procedure 
1. Label the corresponding posts. 
2. Prepare the soil mixture of 50% regolith, 50% garden soil. (75.5 g soil + 75.5g regolith =151g 
total) 
3. Weigh 151 grams of the soil mixture to prepare the kokedamas. 
4. Make a ball with the soil mixture. 
5. Cover the exterior of the soil mixture kokedamas with coconut fiber. (Experimental A) 
6. Cover the exterior of the soil mixture kokedamas with moss fiber. (Experimental B) 
7. Wrap the kokedamas with fishing string to adjust them to the desired size. 
8. Add the corresponding soil mixture (151 grams) to the label pots. 
9. Plant the seeds in the pots and the kokedamas. 
10. Place the pots and the kokedamas in the growing area and set the light period for 12th hours of 
lighting in a 24-hour period. 
11. Proceed to make daily observations and measurements. (Fill your data tables: amount of water, 
humidity, and growth) 
12. After the 8 weeks are done, analyze data, draw conclusions, and prepare the report.

Plant Growth Final Comparison (8 Weeks) 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Humidity Levels Final Comparison (8 Weeks)

Results 
For this experiment we chose how to optimize plant water retention by changing the traditional planting 
method (pot) and replacing it with a kokedama. We have two control groups and two experimental 
groups. In control group A, we utilized a 100% soil mix, and in control group B we used a 50% regolith 50% 
soil mix. On the other hand, our experimental groups are the kokedamas using a 50-50 soil and regolith 
blend, the main difference between the two being the material used for the exterior: experimental group 
A utilizes Coco Fiber while experimental group B utilizes Moss. 
In our first week we encountered problems making the kokedamas correctly, therefore we started 
planting during Week #2. Both Control groups received a total of 250mL of water per plant, with the 
average humidity marking around the 3.6-4.3 range. No growth was present in any control group during 
Week #2. At the same time, the experimental groups were also provided with 250mL of water per plant 
and managed to retain higher levels of water than the control groups. Their average humidity levels 
ranged from 4.7 to 6.2, indicating elevated retention of water which is a good indicator for our hypothesis. 
Nonetheless, there was no growth present in any individual case. 
On Week # 3 we decide to start a new set of kokedamas and change the seeds to Black Simpson Lettuce, 
as the previous Roman Lettuce seeds were not growing, dissenting from previous experiments. 
In Week #4, we finally began to see growth. In Control Group A, Unit 1 is now 4.3cm tall, and Unit 2 is now 
1.5cm tall. Control Group B’s Unit 1 and Unit 2 grew to be 5.5 cm tall. This is a sudden spark in growth, as 
last week there was no verifiable growth. In comparison to the control groups, Week #4 growth in the 
experimental group was slacking. Experimental Group A’s plants grew to be 1.6 and 0.3cm in length, while 
Experimental Group B’s plants grew to be 2 and 0.5cm respectively. As for water distribution, for all 
groups, it remained around 50-150mL. 
Week 5’s Control group levels of humidity were a tad below that of the Experimental Groups. What jumps 
at you from Week 5’s results are the sheer growth of the Experimental Groups. In week #4 the tallest plant 
in the Experimental Groups was 2cm, and now that plant has more than doubled in length, reaching 
4.5cm. The rest of the Experimental Group’s plants reach 5cm and 4.1cm in Group A, and in Group B we 
see 4.5 and 4.8cm respectively. Control Group A’s plants remain relatively the same in terms of growth, 
but Control Group B’s plants shot up to 6.4 and 6cm respectively. For the first time, the water provided at 
times exceeds 150mL and reaches 200mL in all groups except for Experimental B. 
What stands out from the chart of Week #6 is the death of Unit 2 in Control group A. The Unit did not see 
any growth beginning from Friday the week before, culminating with its death exactly a week later. The 
water level in this Unit has been reduced to 100mL for this week alone. If you analyze the growth of this 
unit throughout its entire lifespan, compared to Unit 1 and the other Control Group, this one was always 
falling behind. This may have been an issue that cannot be expressed through the data we have 
documented, such as genetics. Apart from this, the rest of the Control Group’s Units remain growing at a 
constant pace, and on average, the Experimental Groups have, for this week, seen more growth than the 
Control Groups. Both plants in Experimental A surpass all others, marking them as the tallest for now. 
During Week #7, Control Group B catches up with the growth of the kokedamas. Control Group B’s Unit 1 
reaches 9.6cm, the tallest of all plants for now. Control Group A, with its sole survivor, grows up to 8cm.

3 of 4 Experimental units bypass the 9cm threshold, with only Unit 2 of Experimental Group B remaining 
at 7.5. This plant has experienced delayed growth since week #6. Interestingly, Control Group A’s water 
retention reigns supreme in week 7, despite Control Group B receiving the most water out of all groups 
during week 7. 
In our final week, we can see that each Unit in the Control Groups has nearly 2cm in difference. Control 
Group A’s Unit 1 is 10.8 cm tall, while Control Group B’s Unit 1 is 12.1cm, with Unit 2 being 8cm tall. For 
the Experimental Groups, all units present a similar final growth, with both Unit 1s being 11cm, and Group 
A’s Unit 2 being 11.6cm. Unit 2 of Experimental Group B remained stagnant at 8.8cm, as it has been for 3 
weeks at this point. 
With the humidity totals, we can determine that kokedamas were more effective at retaining water than 
normal pots. The final total averages of humidity indicate this, with all but one Unit in the Experimental 
Groups having a greater margin of humidity than the Control Groups. As for the growth, the Experimental 
Groups showed a more consistent growth overall than the Control Groups, as in the Experimental Group 
these numbers remained at around 4.7-5.2cm, but they were comparatively more sporadic in the Control 
Groups. It is also important to accentuate that both Experimental Groups received significantly less water 
than the Control Groups, as it was believed that with less water we would obtain the same results. 
 
Conclusions 
 
At the beginning of the experiment, we were worried about the kokedama’s seeds germinating, since 
kokedama are meant for transplantation, not sowing. Our worries grew further when we saw that the pots 
had germinated before the kokedamas. We felt relieved when we saw the kokedamas germinate the next 
week. We speculate that this late germination was due to the compactness of the kokedama. We saw how 
some of our earlier mud ball prototypes became rock solid when left without water for a while. We have 
concluded that the compactness was most probably due to the use of garden soil in the mixture since it is 
compact in nature. When it comes to water retention, our hypothesis was proven correct because, on 
average, the kokedamas retained more moisture than the pots. We were also pleasantly surprised when 
they grew to be around the same size, even though they germinated a week later and with less water. 
Whether which kokedama (moss or coco fiber) is better at retaining water, we are not sure. The reason we 
are not sure is because the moss has a higher average humidity but also a higher water consumption. The 
difference between the two is also so minimal that it makes it difficult to identify which was more efficient. 
Some of us theorize that the discrepancy has to do with the fact that at the end the moss has bigger plants 
which require more water consumption. Others think that the data is being skewed by the fact that we do 
not have a way to measure the moss’s or the coco fiber’s moisture (we measure the soil inside). But we all 
agree that our hypothesis was correct and the kokedamas had better water retention and subsequently 
the plant grew stronger, healthier, and bigger. We believe the kokedamas are great topic for space research 
because of their accessible and cost-effective materials, perfect shape for storage (they can be hanging or 
just anchored to the floor), and they are versatile.

https://www.domestika.org/en/blog/8650-10-inspiring-examples-of-kokedama-discover-the-art-of-making-
moss-balls 
 
 
Future investigations 
If we were able to make follow up experiments, we would first find out whether the coconut fiber or the 
moss is better at retaining water, repeating the experiment, but this time weighing the same amount of 
both the moss and the coco fiber, increasing the number of samples, and finding a way to measure the 
moisture of the moss or the coco fiber. Next experiment would be to find out what is the most effective 
ratio of regolith to garden soil is for plants to germinate and grow, to try to offset the compactness that 
the garden soil brings to the table. Finally, using the information from the previous experiments, we would 
like to investigate how well transplantation would work and if it is worth it to go through the effort to 
transplant. Of course, this would have to be a long-term project for accurate results.
